```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(ggplot2)

# Figures use the deck's own face. FreeType cannot read the woff2 files the
# browser loads, so slide-tooling ships two static TTF cuts for R. Without
# them the figures fall back to the system sans.
sg_dir <- "fonts/schibsted-grotesk"
fig_family <- "sans"
known <- c(systemfonts::system_fonts()$family, systemfonts::registry_fonts()$family)
if ("Schibsted Grotesk" %in% known) {
  fig_family <- "Schibsted Grotesk"
} else if (file.exists(file.path(sg_dir, "SchibstedGrotesk-Regular.ttf"))) {
  systemfonts::register_font(
    "Schibsted Grotesk",
    plain = file.path(sg_dir, "SchibstedGrotesk-Regular.ttf"),
    bold  = file.path(sg_dir, "SchibstedGrotesk-SemiBold.ttf")
  )
  fig_family <- "Schibsted Grotesk"
}

# Figure palette, matched to the Editorial theme: the vermilion accent for the
# series the slide is about, gray for the comparison, a white ground. If you
# restyle the slide theme, restyle this with it.
col_main <- "#D4371C"
col_soft <- "#8c8c8c"
col_text <- "#5c5c5c"
col_bg   <- "#ffffff"

# base_size 18 sets tick labels near 19px on the slide, since figures are drawn
# at 96 dpi and shown close to 1:1.
talk_theme <- function(base_size = 18) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size, base_family = fig_family) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "#e6e6e6", linewidth = 0.4),
      axis.title = element_text(colour = col_text),
      axis.text = element_text(colour = col_text),
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left",
      legend.title = element_blank(),
      legend.text = element_text(colour = col_text),
      legend.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0),
      plot.margin = margin(2, 6, 2, 2),
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = col_bg, colour = NA)
    )
}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png", dev.args = list(bg = col_bg))
```

## Most prices on this marketplace are now set by software {#intro}

<!-- Clicks: 0 the first line; 1 and 2 one line each, and each earlier line
     grays when the next arrives. -->

::: {.dim-past}
::: {}
- [68%]{.em} of active listings change price at least once a week, against 4% in 2015.
:::
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
- Repricing is delegated to a handful of third-party tools whose rules are published.
:::
::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
- Sellers meet the same rivals week after week, so rules respond to rules.
:::
:::

::: {.aside-note}
Source: PriceScope weekly listing panel, 2015--2023. Own calculations. Online price
competition on this kind of marketplace has been measured since @chevalier2003Measuring.
:::

## Automation pulls prices in two directions at once {#two-forces}

<!-- Clicks: 0 the cost line; 1 the downward force; 2 the upward force; 3 the
     question it leaves. -->

Delegating price setting cuts the cost of a revision from roughly \$14 of seller
attention to near zero.

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
- Cheap revisions let a seller undercut a slow rival within hours, which pushes prices
  [down]{.em} toward marginal cost.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
- Cheap revisions also make undercutting visible and matchable within hours, which
  sustains higher prices when rivals are [equally fast]{.em}.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
Which force dominates depends on the rival mix $\Rival_{mt}$, the share of a market's
listings already under automated pricing.
:::

::: {.aside-note}
Undercutting is the mechanism @chevalier2003Measuring find between two online
booksellers, and the variety it is traded against is what @brynjolfsson2003Consumer
price [see also @chevalier2006Effecta].
:::

## Automation raises prices only where rivals automate too {#claim}

<!-- Clicks: 0 the estimate; 1 the number takes the accent; 2 the reading. -->

::: {.result}
[Headline estimate]{.label}
Adoption raises a listing's price by [6.2 log points]{.fragment .highlight-accent fragment-index=1}
(s.e. 1.4) in the top quartile of rival exposure, and by −0.4 (1.1) in the bottom quartile.
:::

The two estimates come from the same regression, the same sellers, and the same weeks.

::: {.takeaway .fragment fragment-index=2}
Automation is inflationary where it is already common.
:::

## Setting {.section-break}

## API access arrived in a queue, not by application {#queue}

- 41,208 listings in 320 product markets, priced weekly, 2015--2023.
- API access arrived by seller tier, March 2019 to November 2021, with no application
  and no way to move up the queue.
- A listing counts as automated from the first week its price changes on three or more
  distinct days. [Measurement]{.jump target="ap-measure"}

Rival exposure $\Rival_{mt}$ is the share of other listings in market $m$ and week $t$
coded as automated.

::: {.aside-note}
A queue rollout is a design used elsewhere: @wiles2025Algorithmic identify the effect
of algorithmic writing assistance the same way, on hires.
:::

## Adoption tracks the tier queue that granted API access {#adoption}

```{r}
#| label: adoption-curves
#| fig-width: 11.2
#| fig-height: 4.1
base <- subset(economics, date >= as.Date("2000-01-01") & date <= as.Date("2008-12-01"))
n <- nrow(base)
z <- as.numeric(scale(log(base$pce)))

adoption <- data.frame(
  date  = rep(seq(as.Date("2015-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = n), 2),
  share = c(plogis(2.2 * z - 0.8), plogis(2.0 * z - 2.6)),
  grp   = factor(rep(c("Early queue positions", "Late queue positions"), each = n),
                 levels = c("Early queue positions", "Late queue positions"))
)

ggplot(adoption, aes(date, share, colour = grp)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2019-03-01"), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = col_soft, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("text", x = as.Date("2019-06-01"), y = 0.97, hjust = 0, size = 6.2,
           family = fig_family, colour = col_text, label = "Repricing API opens") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(col_main, col_soft)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of listings automated") +
  talk_theme()
```

::: {.aside-note}
Groups are the earliest and latest thirds of the queue, fixed at seller signup. Seller
behaviour on this marketplace has mostly been studied through reviews rather than prices
[@he2022Market].
:::

## Identification {.section-break}

## Identification compares adopters to [not-yet-adopters]{style="white-space:nowrap"} inside the same market-week {#id-equation}

<!-- Clicks: 0 the level term and its note; 1 the interaction; 2 the fixed
     effects; 3 the error, the clustering note, and the assumption. Each layer
     is the whole equation with the terms not yet entered under \class{hid}, so
     nothing moves. -->

::: {.eq-stack}
::: {}
$$\log p_{jmt} = \beta_1 A_{jt}
 \class{hid}{{}+ \class{ac}{\beta_2 \bigl(A_{jt} \times \Rival_{mt}\bigr)}}
 \class{hid}{{}+ \class{gr}{\gamma_j + \delta_{mt}}}
 \class{hid}{{}+ \varepsilon_{jmt}}$$
:::
::: {.eq-layer .fragment fragment-index=1}
$$\log p_{jmt} = \beta_1 A_{jt}
 {}+ \class{ac}{\beta_2 \bigl(A_{jt} \times \Rival_{mt}\bigr)}
 \class{hid}{{}+ \class{gr}{\gamma_j + \delta_{mt}}}
 \class{hid}{{}+ \varepsilon_{jmt}}$$
:::
::: {.eq-layer .fragment fragment-index=2}
$$\log p_{jmt} = \beta_1 A_{jt}
 {}+ \class{ac}{\beta_2 \bigl(A_{jt} \times \Rival_{mt}\bigr)}
 {}+ \class{gr}{\gamma_j + \delta_{mt}}
 \class{hid}{{}+ \varepsilon_{jmt}}$$
:::
::: {.eq-layer .fragment fragment-index=3}
$$\log p_{jmt} = \beta_1 A_{jt}
 {}+ \class{ac}{\beta_2 \bigl(A_{jt} \times \Rival_{mt}\bigr)}
 {}+ \class{gr}{\gamma_j + \delta_{mt}}
 {}+ \varepsilon_{jmt}$$
:::
:::

::: {.eq-notes}
::: {}
$A_{jt} \in \{0,1\}$ marks automation; $\beta_1$ is the level effect.
:::
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
$\beta_2$ is how the effect grows with the share of rivals already automated.
:::
::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
$\gamma_j$ absorbs the listing and $\delta_{mt}$ the market-week.
:::
::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
Standard errors are clustered by market.
:::
:::

::: {.assumption .fragment fragment-index=3}
[Parallel trends given exposure.]{.label} Given rival exposure, adoption timing carries
no information about the untreated price path.
:::

## Estimates {.section-break}

## The level effect is a wash; the interaction is not {#table}

::: {.regtable}
| Outcome: log price | Pooled | + Market × week FE | Interaction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Automated pricing | 0.024 | 0.019 | −0.004 |
|   | (0.008) | (0.009) | (0.011) |
| Automation × top-quartile rival exposure |  |  | [0.066]{.em} |
|   |  |  | (0.017) |
| Market × week fixed effects | No | Yes | Yes |
| Listings | 41,208 | 41,208 | 41,208 |
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
Pooling across markets averages a positive and a zero effect into a small positive one.
:::

## Mechanism {.section-break}

## Complementarity follows from the slope of the best response {#proposition}

<!-- Clicks: 0 the proposition; 1 the proof; 2 the reading. -->

::: {.proposition}
[Proposition 1.]{.label}
Let $\pi_j(p_j, p_{-j})$ be log-concave in $p_j$ and suppose automation lowers the
adjustment cost $\kappa_j$. If $\partial^2 \pi_j / \partial p_j \partial p_{-j} > 0$, then
$p_j^\star = \argmax_p \pi_j(p, p_{-j}) - \kappa_j \mathbf{1}\{p \neq p_{j,t-1}\}$ is
increasing in $p_{-j}$, and adoption decisions are strategic complements.
:::

::: {.proof .fragment fragment-index=1}
Log-concavity gives a unique interior maximizer, so $p_j^\star$ is characterized by the
first-order condition. Falling $\kappa_j$ widens the region where the constraint
$p = p_{j,t-1}$ does not bind, and on that region the cross-partial signs
$\mathrm{d} p_j^\star / \mathrm{d} p_{-j} > 0$ by Topkis.
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment fragment-index=2}
The empirical interaction is the comparative static the model predicts.
:::

## Three checks bound the demand-selection threat {#threats}

<!-- Clicks: 0 the threat; 1 to 3 one check each, earlier checks gray. The IV
     button arrives with the second check, which it qualifies. -->

Sellers who automate first may be facing rising demand, which would raise prices with or
without the API.

::: {.dim-past}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
- Adoption timing is [uncorrelated]{.em} with pre-period price and quantity trends
  once tier is held fixed ($p = 0.71$).
:::
::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
- Within-tier queue position, set by a signup date years earlier, gives the same
  interaction: 0.059 (0.022). [IV]{.jump target="ap-iv"}
:::
::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
- Rival exposure is [not]{.em} predicted by own-market demand growth.
:::
:::

::: {.aside-note}
A market-level shock hitting exposure and prices in the same week remains open. Demand
dynamics on platforms of this kind are modelled directly by @yin2024MetaLearning.
:::

## Policy {.section-break}

## A composition test is what a regulator can actually run {#composition}

<!-- Clicks: 0 the unavailable inputs; 1 swapped in place for the available
     one; 2 the two regimes. -->

::: {.swap}
::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
A regulator could be asked to observe the pricing algorithms, which are private, or to
prove intent, which is unfalsifiable. Neither is available.
:::
::: {.swap-in .fragment fragment-index=1}
This test asks for the share of a market already automated, which the platform records
and publishes. That is the whole input.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
- Below roughly a 40% automated share, permitting automation moves prices by nothing we
  can distinguish from zero.
- Above it, the same permission is worth 4 to 7 log points, [rising in the share]{.em}.
:::

::: {.aside-note}
The threshold is where the fitted interaction crosses zero, so it inherits the standard
error on the interaction. Whether firms adopt in the first place is a separate question
[@dietvorst2018Overcoming; @brynjolfsson2025Generative].
:::

## Takeaways {#takeaways .closing-slide}

1. Automated pricing has no single price effect. It raises prices by [6.2 log points]{.em}
   (s.e. 1.4) in the top quartile of rival exposure and by −0.4 (1.1) in the bottom.
2. The interaction is the comparative static a model with strategic complements predicts.
3. A regulator can test market composition, the share of a market already automated,
   which the platform already records and publishes.

## Robustness to the sample window {#ap-window}

::: {.spec}
| Sample or specification | Interaction | s.e. | Level effect | Listings | Markets | Pre-trend $p$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Baseline, 2015--2023 | 0.066 | 0.017 | −0.004 | 41,208 | 320 | 0.71 |
| Post-API weeks only, 2019--2023 | 0.071 | 0.021 | −0.002 | 33,415 | 320 | 0.64 |
| Drop the 2020 demand spike | 0.070 | 0.018 | −0.002 | 38,940 | 320 | 0.69 |
| Drop the last adoption cohort | 0.061 | 0.023 | −0.006 | 29,884 | 311 | 0.55 |
| Market-specific linear trends | 0.058 | 0.026 | −0.005 | 41,208 | 320 | 0.83 |
:::

Nothing here moves the estimate by more than half a standard error.

[]{.jump-back}

## Why we do not instrument adoption with tier eligibility {#ap-iv}

Tier eligibility is a valid instrument for own adoption and a [weak]{.em} one for the
interaction, because the first stage for $A_{jt} \times \Rival_{mt}$ requires exogenous
variation in both arguments at once. The available instrument moves only the first.

The reduced form is reported instead: crossing an eligibility threshold raises price by
0.031 (0.012) in high-exposure markets and 0.002 (0.010) elsewhere, a ratio close to the
interaction estimate scaled by the 0.48 first stage.

::: {.aside-note}
A two-sample approach using a second platform's queue is in progress.
:::

[]{.jump-back}

## How automated pricing is measured {#ap-measure}

The three-distinct-days rule is the middle of three thresholds. Tighter and looser rules
move the classified share, but not the estimate.

::: {.spec}
| Classification rule | Share | Changes per week | Interaction | s.e. | Listings |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Price changes on two or more distinct days | 0.71 | 2.4 | 0.061 | 0.015 | 41,208 |
| Three or more distinct days (baseline) | 0.54 | 3.6 | 0.066 | 0.017 | 41,208 |
| Four or more distinct days | 0.39 | 4.5 | 0.072 | 0.020 | 41,208 |
:::

::: {.aside-note}
No listing in the 2015--2018 pre-period crosses the three-day rule for more than two
consecutive weeks. Imputing the level a listing would have been assigned under an
unobserved rule follows @bradlow2004LearningBased; richer platform data would allow the
approach of @gabel2024Market or the features surveyed in @grewal2021Marketing, and letting
a model propose the rule is the case @ludwig2024Machine make.
:::
